The Eastern Orthodox Church. One of the three major branches of Christianity, the Eastern Orthodox Church has roots in the apostolic churches of the Eastern Mediterranean and the Byzantine Empire. After the Great Schism of 1054 separated it from the Roman Catholic Church, Orthodoxy developed distinctive theology, liturgy, and iconography centered on Constantinople and later Russia. It remains the dominant Christian tradition in Eastern Europe, Russia, and parts of the Middle East today.

The Eastern Orthodox Church traces its apostolic succession to Jesus's disciples and the early churches of Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria, and Constantinople. It differs from Roman Catholicism in rejecting papal supremacy, in its approach to the veneration of icons—which was eventually accepted after the Iconoclastic Controversy—and in certain doctrinal emphases. The Great Schism in 1054 formalized the split between Eastern, Byzantine, Orthodox Christianity and Western Roman Catholicism over jurisdiction and theology.

The Byzantine Empire was intimately identified with Orthodoxy; the Church provided spiritual legitimacy to imperial rule and preserved Greek learning. After Constantinople's fall in 1453, Moscow became the "Third Rome," positioning Russian Orthodoxy as the tradition's center and successor to Byzantine Christianity. The church survived Ottoman conquest and suppression during the Ottoman centuries from 1453 onwards, maintaining identity under foreign rule. The Iconoclastic Controversy in the eighth and ninth centuries saw emperors suppress icon veneration, but the eventual restoration of icons became a defining Orthodox doctrine distinguishing it from Western Christianity.

The Eastern Orthodox Church today claims approximately 300 million adherents, concentrated in Russia, Ukraine, Serbia, Greece, and the Middle East, with significant diaspora communities worldwide. The Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople remains the symbolic leader of Orthodoxy, though Orthodox churches are autocephalous, or self-governing, creating a decentralized structure contrasting sharply with papal Catholicism. This church uses the Divine Liturgy, or Eucharist, as its central practice, emphasizing mystery, image through icons, and the transfiguration of matter as sacred.
